Buying Short Line would give me three railroads and $100 in rent, but four would be needed to beat player two's B&O. The final counter-offer is $100 cash for both Vermont and Oriental. I will explain that the $260 offer is too rich because Oriental is mortgaged, and I will not fund player one's red builds.

I am weighing whether to reject the trade outright or counter with $100. Rejecting would preserve my liquidity and the Connecticut block, but it might let player one sell the properties to someone else. Only I can complete the light blue set, so the properties are most valuable as a monopoly.

I now see that only I can complete the light blue set, giving me strong leverage. Player one is desperate for cash to build red houses. I will counter with $80 or $100 and request both properties. I cannot force them to unmortgage Oriental through the trade schema. I am also reconsidering whether to accept the full $260 offer.

A light blue monopoly is my only current path to a monopoly. Four houses would cost $230 and leave a $30 buffer, but even-build rules forbid putting all four on one street. One house each would yield only $30–40 in rent, which is too weak. Player one would jump to two houses on reds and likely hit me before I could build. The expected value is negative, so I will not accept the trade. A $200 counter-offer would still leave player one with enough cash to buy one red house.

The counter-offer is now fixed at $100 cash for both Vermont and Oriental. This leaves player one with exactly $148, which is below the $150 threshold needed to buy a red house. I will not fund their red builds.

A formal counter is preferable to a simple rejection. Player one has been persistent, having already offered $320 and $260 before. A clear lowball of $100 signals genuine interest while keeping the price too low to fund their red builds. Earlier rejections were made while saving for Tennessee; now I actually want the set cheaply.

The public message will be brief and firm, stating that $100 is the take-it-or-leave-it offer because Oriental is mortgaged. I am also rechecking whether accepting the full $260 could ever be justified, since paying it would leave me with $285 in cash.

Even with four evenly spaced houses on the light blue set, rent would still be too weak to compete with player one's red monopoly. Player one could also mortgage Vermont to fund two houses on the reds, leaving them at 2-2-2. They have no other unmortgaged properties to mortgage.

I am calculating how much cash I would need to build three houses on the light blue set. Even with four evenly spaced houses, rent would only reach $450, which is still too weak to compete with player one's red monopoly. I do have enough mortgage capacity across my other properties to fund that build.
